# Beyond the hype of Robotic Process Automation (RPA): on conditions needed to implement RPA in organizations

- Original Article
- Open access
- Published: 31 March 2026

- Duc-Minh-Quan Huynh 1 & 
- Ida Lindgren 2 

## Abstract

Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is often marketed as a lightweight and easy-to-implement solution for process automation. However, this portrayal can be misleading. Our study reveals that RPA implementation shares many complexities with more comprehensive automation technologies, requiring strategic planning and organizational commitment. Through a systematic literature review following PRISMA and Kitchenham guidelines, we identify 12 organizational challenges to RPA implementation using the TOE framework and derive 7 sequential technical, organizational, and strategic conditions for its successful adoption. Four key insights include: RPA implementation (1) demands deep technical knowledge of both RPA tools and the existing digital infrastructure; (2) requires specific organizational and process-related capabilities; (3) involves multiple actors with distinct roles across 2022pre- and post-implementation phases; and (4) depends on clear policies and governance strategies. These findings highlight the importance of moving beyond simplistic narratives of RPA adoption and recognizing the multifaceted conditions that shape its success. Our review also identifies research gaps, including the need for studies on designing governance frameworks, aligning automation technologies with different process types, and supporting hybrid human-automation solutions. The role of RPA enthusiasts in driving adoption also emerges as a critical but underexplored area. This study contributes a nuanced understanding of RPA implementation challenges and offers practical insights for organizations navigating process automation. It serves as a resource for both researchers and practitioners aiming to better prepare for the technical, organizational, and strategic demands of RPA.

## 1 Introduction

Workplace technologies have evolved significantly over the past few decades—from standalone office applications in the 1980 s to today’s digitally connected platforms embedded with automation and AI-driven self-learning capabilities (Lyytinen et al. 2021). This progression marks more than a shift in tools; it represents a fundamental transformation in how work is performed, coordinated, and understood. In modern organizations, intelligent automation tools—ranging from rule-based systems to AI-powered decision engines—are reshaping not only operational processes but also the social fabric and managerial dynamics of the workplace (Coombs et al. 2020).

These technologies are no longer limited to supporting tasks or streamlining operations. They serve as catalysts for rethinking how value is delivered, how roles are defined, and how organizations evolve (Baptista et al. 2020; Coombs et al. 2020). Increasingly, digital tools are embedded into the core of organizational functioning, influencing how people interact, how decisions are made, and how work identities are formed. Human–technology configurations are becoming more complex and dynamic, requiring continuous assembly and reassembly by individuals who often operate without formal recognition (Baptista et al. 2020). This invisible work, what (Baptista et al. 2020) call strategic configuration work, is crucial in determining whether technology integration leads to superficial optimization or deeper organizational transformation.

To understand these deeper impacts, (Baptista et al. 2020) propose a layered framework of first-, second-, and third-order effects. First-order effects involve immediate efficiency gains and task improvements. Second-order effects bring changes to roles and work design, while third-order effects alter the very identity, strategy, and capabilities of an organization. These latter changes emerge through the cumulative and often hidden efforts of individuals managing the evolving digital/human configurations. As newer, more advanced technologies are layered onto existing systems, these configurations become increasingly complex, and so does the work required to manage them. Yet, the nature of this configuration of work, how it should be carried out, and the conditions necessary for its success often remain unrecognized, under-reported, and poorly understood, leading to drift, misalignment, and increased organizational risk (Baptista et al. 2020).

Robotic Process Automation (RPA) exemplifies this phenomenon. Within this broader digital transformation landscape, RPA has emerged as a widely adopted intelligent automation tool and a new type of workplace technology. The technology plays a key role, alongside various artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the process automation advancements, contributing to the emergence of what is sometimes referred to as Industry 4.0 (Ribeiro et al. 2021). Automation, in general, can be defined as “the execution by a machine agent (usually a computer) of a function that was previously carried out by a human” (Parasuraman and Riley 1997, p. 231). Process automation, as addressed here, is a narrower concept, targeting the automation of administrative procedures in organizations using various digital technologies.

RPA, introduced around 2010, is still considered a relatively new technology. In the IEEE guide on intelligent process automation, RPA is described as “neither an operating system nor an application, but a platform built to provide digital process automation that mimics human operations in a digital environment”. Furthermore, “it can use single or multiple applications or systems through the standard human interface layer, in the same way a human operator would” (IEEE Corporate Advisory Group 2017). For example, RPA has been adopted to support case workers in the public sector, with the aim of improving efficiency while facing increasing workloads and limited budgets (Toll et al. 2022). RPA has also been adopted to handle administrative processes related to payroll, purchasing, recruitment, and healthcare claims; in diverse types of industries, e.g., finance and insurance, oil and gas, logistics, and healthcare (Ivančić et al. 2019). In 2019, according to Statista (2019), 49% of large companies globally had invested in RPA, with 24% already integrating this technology into their operations. SMEs have also caught on this trend, where 14% of small-sized and 17% of mid-sized companies have invested in RPA, while 9% of both groups have adopted it into their workflows (ibid.). Many studies have served to investigate potential uses, merits, and pitfalls of RPA in various types of organizations and for different types of processes (e.g, Aguirre and Rodriguez 2017; Noppen et al. 2020; Willcocks and Lacity 2016). There is also a growing body of literature on RPA use and its impacts in the public sector (e.g., Asatiani 2022; Borry and Getha-Taylor 2019; Germundsson 2022; Veale and Brass 2019). Marketing materials from RPA vendors present it as fast, cost-efficient, scalable, and easy to use—requiring no programming skills (Toll and Söderström 2020).

However, this idealized narrative often diverges from real-world experiences. Empirical studies show that RPA implementations can be time-consuming, resource-intensive, and technically demanding, particularly in public sector contexts (Hindel et al. 2020; Lindgren et al. 2022, 2024; Johansson et al. 2023). For example, empirical studies of RPA implementations in the Swedish public sector (e.g., Johansson et al. 2023; Lindgren et al. 2024), have showed the opposite, namely that (1) RPA implementations tend to be time-consuming and exceed budget; (2) RPA solutions are difficult to configure and use without IT skills; (3) these systems fit poorly with the existing IT-infrastructure in these organizations; and (4) the efficiency gains are unclear and difficult to assess. Issues such as these are not only reported by public organizations (Eikebrokk and Olsen 2020). In fact, many organizations seem to struggle to make successful use of RPA and various studies have reported a multitude of organizational factors as key barriers hindering the success of RPA implementation. However, studies are scarce that collate RPA challenges and draw conclusions on what these challenges mean in terms of organizational conditions required for RPA implementation. This is a gap in the literature that we wish to fill.

This paper contributes to the strategic information systems discourse by examining organizational conditions that are not only critical for the successful implementation of RPA, but also essential for helping organizations navigate the deeper second- and third-order effects of digital transformation, such as shifts in roles, strategy, and organizational identity. Building on recent contributions of Baptista et al. (2020) and Coombs et al. (2020), we argue that understanding RPA’s role in digital transformation demands a nuanced perspective, one that goes beyond technical capabilities to consider how RPA interacts with organizational structures, values, and strategic goals. Accordingly, the aim of this study is to develop a comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the challenges associated with RPA implementation and to identify the organizational conditions necessary for its successful adoption. This aim is addressed through the following two research questions:

RQ1: What organizational challenges and barriers are experienced in relation to RPA use and implementation?

RQ2: What technical, organizational, and strategic conditions are required for the successful implementation of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in organizations?

The first research question is examined through the lens of the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework. By systematically investigating the current body of literature on RPA use and implementation, we identify and structure lessons learned that can inform guidelines for organizations interested in process automation, as well as highlight research gaps that should be addressed in future studies, thus addressing the second research question.

The structure of the paper is as follows. Following the introduction, in Sect. 2, we provide a more detailed description of RPA, including existing research on this topic, as well as the theoretical framework used in the study. In Sect. 3, we present the structured review method used to generate and analyze the literature. This is followed by a presentation of our findings in Sect. 4, and a subsequent discussion of what these findings mean for RPA practice and research. Last, in Sect. 6, we provide a set of conclusions, discuss limitations, and make recommendations for future research.

## 2 Background and framing

To better understand why RPA implementation is challenging to implement and what organizational conditions are needed to successfully work with RPA, we must first unpack what makes RPA a special form of process automation. We then proceed to provide a theoretical framing for the analysis of the literature, in the shape of the technology-organization-environment (TOE) framework.

### 2.1 Robotic Process Automation

RPA is a specific type of software that can be programmed to perform structured work tasks (Penttinen et al. 2018) by imitating human users’ interactions in one or several systems (Lacity and Willcocks 2021), e.g., commands, mouse clicks, and transferring data between different systems and platforms (Aguirre and Rodriguez 2017).
